power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

From Echo Chambers to Echo Machines?
text.formatted: <head>From Echo Chambers to Echo Machines?

text.text: Endorsement, Evidence, and the Certainty of Belief in Conversations With AI
text.formatted: Endorsement, Evidence, and the Certainty of Belief in Conversations With AI</head>

text.text: Conversations with large language models (LLMs) can move beliefs in opposite directions.

In randomized studies, dialogues with chatbots reduced conspiracy belief and, more modestly, political polarization (Costello et al., 2024; Costello, Pennycook, & Rand, 2026; Hruschka & Appel, in press; Kim et al., 2026; Walter, 2025).
text.formatted: In randomized studies, dialogues with chatbots reduced conspiracy belief and, more modestly, political polarization <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Costello et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Costello, Pennycook, & Rand, 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Hruschka & Appel, in press;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Kim et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Walter, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Instructed to promote conspiracy theories, the same systems increased belief (Costello, Pelrine, et al., 2026), and clinical reports describe escalating implausible convictions during intensive chatbot use, without establishing causality (Morrin et al., 2026; Østergaard, 2023).
text.formatted: Instructed to promote conspiracy theories, the same systems increased belief <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Costello, Pelrine, et al., 2026)</ref>, and clinical reports describe escalating implausible convictions during intensive chatbot use, without establishing causality <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Morrin et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Østergaard, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: A third possibility has received less attention: a conversation may leave what someone believes almost unchanged, or even moderate it, while making the belief more certain and therefore harder to revise.
The question extends a debate that has focused on social-media feeds and the echo chambers they are thought to create, often described as centrifugal forces that push opinions apart.

Large field experiments around the 2020 U.S. presidential election found little change in polarization after altering feed ranking or reducing exposure to like-minded sources (Guess et al., 2023; Nyhan et al., 2023), but they changed what people saw, not the approval attached to it.
text.formatted: Large field experiments around the 2020 U.S. presidential election found little change in polarization after altering feed ranking or reducing exposure to like-minded sources <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Guess et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Nyhan et al., 2023)</ref>, but they changed what people saw, not the approval attached to it.

text.text: A chatbot's reply carries both information about the world and approval of the user, and the two can be manipulated separately.
Prominent accounts of AI persuasion are information-centered.

In one, factual content drives belief change in either direction (Costello, Pelrine, et al., 2026; Costello, Pennycook, & Rand, 2026); in another, sycophancy is formalized as biased sampling of evidence, which can make even a perfectly rational reasoner overconfident (Batista & Griffiths, 2026; Chandra et al., 2026).
text.formatted: In one, factual content drives belief change in either direction <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Costello, Pelrine, et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Costello, Pennycook, & Rand, 2026)</ref>; in another, sycophancy is formalized as biased sampling of evidence, which can make even a perfectly rational reasoner overconfident <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Batista & Griffiths, 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Chandra et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: In both, a message acts by supplying evidence.
Yet a reply also tells people that they are right and that their position is reasonable.
Most trials confound this endorsement with evidence, and the clearest attempt to separate them favored the factual pathway (Rathje et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Most trials confound this endorsement with evidence, and the clearest attempt to separate them favored the factual pathway <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Rathje et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: We ask two separable questions.
Does endorsement raise the certainty of a belief when factual content is held constant?
And does certainty so raised reduce responsiveness to later counterevidence?
The most discriminating test uses a chatbot that participants know approves everyone.
Its approval carries little information about whether one is right; if it nevertheless raises certainty and dampens later updating, purely informational accounts become harder to sustain.

Social psychology has long studied attitude certainty, self-validation, and flattery; conversational AI makes it possible to separate the evidential and social functions of agreement, at scale and in private.
We review the relevant social psychology, propose a minimal model, read existing trials through it, derive experiments, and close with clinical and design implications.
Research on attitude strength distinguishes the position of an attitude from the certainty with which it is held.

Attitude certainty, the subjective sense that one's attitude is clear and correct, is distinct from extremity and predicts resistance to persuasion and attitude-behavior consistency (Tormala & Rucker, 2007).
text.formatted: Attitude certainty, the subjective sense that one's attitude is clear and correct, is distinct from extremity and predicts resistance to persuasion and attitude-behavior consistency <ref type="bibr">(Tormala & Rucker, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: It has at least two components: clarity, knowing what one thinks, and correctness, believing that it is right; perceived consensus particularly affects correctness (Petrocelli et al., 2007).
text.formatted: It has at least two components: clarity, knowing what one thinks, and correctness, believing that it is right; perceived consensus particularly affects correctness <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Petrocelli et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: A moderate attitude can thus be held with great certainty, a dissociation that measures of polarization, which usually record position alone, cannot detect.
Certainty also responds to inputs that carry little information about the attitude object.

According to the self-validation hypothesis, confidence in one's thoughts, not only their content, determines their influence, so variables unrelated to argument quality can change persuasion (Petty et al., 2002).
text.formatted: According to the self-validation hypothesis, confidence in one's thoughts, not only their content, determines their influence, so variables unrelated to argument quality can change persuasion <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Petty et al., 2002)</ref>.

text.text: Successfully resisting a persuasive attack can itself increase certainty (Tormala & Petty, 2002), which implies that a counterargument used to probe certainty can also change it.
text.formatted: Successfully resisting a persuasive attack can itself increase certainty <ref type="bibr">(Tormala & Petty, 2002)</ref>, which implies that a counterargument used to probe certainty can also change it.

text.text: Social sources of confidence appear in several literatures.

People give more weight to their own opinion than to advice, especially advice far from their view (Bonaccio & Dalal, 2006; Yaniv, 2004), and seek feedback that confirms how they see themselves (Swann et al., 1989).
text.formatted: People give more weight to their own opinion than to advice, especially advice far from their view <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Bonaccio & Dalal, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Yaniv, 2004)</ref>, and seek feedback that confirms how they see themselves <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Swann et al., 1989)</ref>.

text.text: On a news aggregator, a single randomized positive rating increased the probability of further positive ratings by 32% (Muchnik et al., 2013).
text.formatted: On a news aggregator, a single randomized positive rating increased the probability of further positive ratings by 32% <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Muchnik et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Not every link between consensus and confidence implies influence, however: shared views are expressed more confidently even without social influence, plausibly because they rest on more consistent considerations (Koriat et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Not every link between consensus and confidence implies influence, however: shared views are expressed more confidently even without social influence, plausibly because they rest on more consistent considerations <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Koriat et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: The experiments proposed below therefore manipulate endorsement rather than merely measure it.
Two findings concern sources known to be uninformative.

Praise from a computer that participants were told was unrelated to their performance still improved their self-evaluations (Fogg & Nass, 1997), and flattery recognized as insincere still left favorable implicit evaluations of the flatterer (Chan & Sengupta, 2010).
text.formatted: Praise from a computer that participants were told was unrelated to their performance still improved their self-evaluations <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Fogg & Nass, 1997)</ref>, and flattery recognized as insincere still left favorable implicit evaluations of the flatterer <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Chan & Sengupta, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Approval known to carry no information may act below the level at which it is discounted.
Individual differences should matter as much as situations, and they may act at different points.

The need for cognitive closure disposes people to seize and freeze on available answers (Kruglanski & Webster, 1996), self-uncertainty motivates identification with groups that offer clear, consensual beliefs (Hogg, 2007), and a tendency to anthropomorphize may lend approval from a machine the weight of approval from a mind (Waytz et al., 2010); all three could amplify the initial effect of endorsement on certainty.

text.text: Intellectual humility, the recognition that one's views may be wrong (Leary et al., 2017), may instead govern whether certainty, once raised, turns into resistance, although a humble person can still be sensitive to social approval.
text.formatted: Intellectual humility, the recognition that one's views may be wrong <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Leary et al., 2017)</ref>, may instead govern whether certainty, once raised, turns into resistance, although a humble person can still be sensitive to social approval.

text.text: Need for cognition makes a less obvious prediction: because self-validation effects are most likely when people process information extensively (Petty et al., 2002), endorsement may raise certainty most among those who think most, unless careful thinking also sharpens scrutiny of the approval itself.
text.formatted: Need for cognition makes a less obvious prediction: because self-validation effects are most likely when people process information extensively <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Petty et al., 2002)</ref>, endorsement may raise certainty most among those who think most, unless careful thinking also sharpens scrutiny of the approval itself.

text.text: Endorsement may therefore act on certainty, on the value of holding a belief, or on both, and to different degrees in different people.
Approval-induced certainty has a long history in social psychology.

What has not, to our knowledge, been combined is non-probative approval, certainty measured independently of position, and the subsequent response to standardized counterevidence, in a dialogue in which the approving source can also supply evidence.
We propose a descriptive model (Figure 1A), meant to organize competing predictions rather than to describe a neural process or an ideal of rational inference.
text.formatted: We propose a descriptive model (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1A</ref>), meant to organize competing predictions rather than to describe a neural process or an ideal of rational inference.

text.text: A belief has two properties: its position, what is believed (for example, how strongly a claim is endorsed), and its certainty, how firmly that position is held.
Each reply from a chatbot contains two components.
Evidence bears on which position is correct; endorsement affirms the person or the position independently of argument content, through agreement, praise, or reassurance.
Endorsement can be epistemic ("you are right to think that") or interpersonal ("I understand why this matters to you"), and the two may act differently.
Evidence moves the position, and it also changes certainty: confirming evidence raises it and disconfirming evidence lowers it.
Because confirmation is judged relative to the position currently held, a person who changes their mind can rebuild certainty around the new position.
On this baseline, the model adds two hypotheses that can be tested, and can fail, separately.
The first (H1) is a validation effect: endorsement raises certainty directly, beyond any evidence it contains.
The second (H2) is that higher certainty reduces the weight given to later evidence.
H2 is a substantive psychological assumption rather than a consequence of how certainty is defined; it is the link that would turn a momentary gain in confidence into lasting rigidity.
A formal version of the model, with illustrative simulations, is given in the Supplementary Material; the argument does not depend on it.
Empirically, a validation effect is an effect of endorsement on certainty at fixed factual content.
Its existence would leave the underlying mechanism open.

Endorsement can signal the quality of one's reasoning, improve mood or self-efficacy, or increase the value of holding a belief, and one can argue that even agreement from an uninformed source carries some information, because agreement is more likely when one is right.
An approver known to agree with everyone makes that inference less plausible without eliminating it.

We therefore separate three claims: (a) a randomized effect of endorsement on certainty at constant factual content; (b) an effect not statistically accounted for by measured informational and other mediators; and (c) its psychological mechanism.
The experiments target the first, examine the second under explicit assumptions, and leave the third as a research program.
Certainty and resistance to revision may also come apart.
A person can feel certain yet yield to a strong argument, and can hold on to a position for reasons of identity without feeling sure that it is true.

A motivational alternative is accordingly that approval makes a belief more comfortable or identity-affirming rather than more certain; greater resistance without greater reported confidence, especially if attenuated by incentives for accuracy, would favor it.
Conversely, approval that raises certainty without reducing later revision would support H1 while refuting H2, an informative result in its own right.

The central implication follows from combining the two hypotheses: if endorsement raises certainty and certainty lowers the weight of later evidence, approval now can make counterevidence later less effective.
Figure 1B illustrates this temporal prediction with chosen parameters, not estimates: after a phase of approval, the same counterevidence moves the position less than after a neutral exchange.

text.text: A belief can thus become more rigid without becoming more extreme, with no false information supplied.
Articulation can also change certainty before any reply.

Explaining how a mechanism works can reveal an illusion of explanatory depth and moderate extreme positions, whereas justifying a position may increase its apparent coherence (Fernbach et al., 2013; Rozenblit & Keil, 2002).

Most conversational trials deliver arguments and endorsement in the same messages and cannot separate the two channels, but they set the baseline against which any validation effect must be judged.

The capacity to contradict comes with the capacity to agree.

Preference-trained LLMs can favor agreeable over accurate responses, partly because people sometimes prefer convincing sycophantic answers to correct ones (Sharma et al., 2024), and across 11 models, LLMs preserved users' self-image about 45 percentage points more often than humans did (Cheng, Yu, et al., 2026).

text.text: The open question is whether endorsement adds anything beyond biased sampling.
The closest direct evidence is challenging for our account.

text.text: A small or null validation effect is thus a serious possibility.
The narrower question we pursue is whether any residual change in certainty predicts the uptake of later counterevidence.
Such an effect would be invisible in designs that measure position and confidence only once.
Feeds and chatbots may also differ in the direction of their influence.

Engagement-driven feeds select content from behavioral traces such as likes and dwell time, largely without access to why users believe what they believe, and expose them to peer endorsement before an audience (Kahan, 2013; Muchnik et al., 2013), conditions often thought to push opinions apart.

text.text: A conversational model receives the user's reasons and can answer them individually, privately, and with counterevidence targeted at the claims the user cites.

Recent studies suggest a centripetal pull: dialogues with chatbots reduced conspiracy beliefs, issue polarization, and cross-partisan animosity (Costello et al., 2024; Hruschka & Appel, in press; Lira Luttges et al., 2026), although some effects faded within weeks.

text.text: In an audit of six widely used chatbots, all disputed election conspiracy theories under repeated pushback while remaining sympathetic toward the skeptical user (Brennan Center for Justice, 2026).
That combination, factual contradiction delivered with interpersonal validation, is precisely the one our account singles out.
A centripetal influence on positions is compatible with a parallel rise in certainty: users may leave such conversations with more moderate positions, held more firmly.
Whether conversational AI fosters epistemic flexibility therefore depends on certainty as well as on position.
Dialogue also provides the means to find out, because facts, affirmation, and their sequence can be varied independently in a way that is difficult on a feed.
An information-centered account predicts that endorsement operates only through perceived evidence, source reliability, or diagnostic feedback about one's reasoning.
The two-channel account predicts an endorsement effect on certainty at identical factual content (H1), followed by reduced responsiveness to counterevidence (H2).
Affect-and identity-based alternatives can also predict residual effects, so the experiments test both hypotheses against specified alternatives (Table 2).

text.text: Position, certainty, and resistance must be measured separately.

On a bounded scale, a rating of 95 out of 100 can express a strong position held tentatively or a moderate one held firmly; confidence that one's rating is correct, attitude clarity, and attitude correctness can be measured apart from the rating (Petrocelli et al., 2007).

text.text: Resistance is the proportional shift after a standardized counterargument, identical across arms, relative to the remaining distance to the counterargument's position.
In the model, confidence and resistance move together; resistance without confidence would point to identity or motivation.
Because resisting a probe can itself increase certainty (Tormala & Petty, 2002), measurement order should be counterbalanced.

text.text: Credibility, affect, and belief value measured after the intervention are potential mediators, not baseline controls.
The first experiment tests H1.

It crosses factual evidence (present vs. absent) with endorsement (high vs. low) in replies matched for length and fluency, with endorsement framed as epistemic agreement or as interpersonal validation (Li et al., 2026; Ye et al., 2026).

text.text: A neutral restatement controls for re-exposure to one's own opinion.
Two further conditions describe the source as having no access to the facts or as approving everyone.
The latter is the most discriminating condition: it sharply reduces, without eliminating, the diagnostic value of agreement.
Primary outcomes are changes in confidence or attitude correctness and the later proportional update after a standardized counterargument.
The second experiment tests H2 and the temporal prediction.
Participants receive identical counterevidence after either a phase of explicitly non-probative endorsement or a matched neutral interaction; a third arm reverses the order.

The counterevidence comes from a source distinct from the endorsing chatbot, because contradiction by the same chatbot could lower its credibility independently of any change in certainty, and the interval before the counterevidence is identical across arms.
The prediction is that endorsement raises certainty and that raised certainty predicts less revision.
Attention, memory, and source-inconsistency accounts remain competitors.

Before any chatbot reply, a control randomizes writing an explanation of a mechanism, a justification of one's position, or a neutral text, so that effects of composing the prompt are not misattributed to AI feedback; writing one's reasons has already been associated with reduced conspiracy belief in an uncontrolled pre-post study (Meyer et al., 2024).

text.text: Scripted replies rated by blind coders hold evidence constant at some cost in ecological validity; a hybrid design, in which a live model supplies fixed evidence and endorsement is added by a separate step, offers a compromise.
Participants should demonstrate, before the manipulation, that they understand that the source approves everyone, and analyses should be by intention to treat.
A participant who understands this and still finds the approval meaningful is precisely the case of interest.

If the validation effect is small, as the closest evidence suggests, studies must be powered for small effects, with a preregistered smallest effect of interest and equivalence tests to establish whether it is negligible rather than merely undetected.

Individual differences can be measured before randomization with brief validated scales, such as the 15-item Need for Closure Scale (Roets & Van Hiel, 2011), the Intellectual Humility Scale (Leary et al., 2017), and a measure of anthropomorphism (Waytz et al., 2010).

text.text: These traits may moderate the two pathways independently: anthropomorphism and need for closure may influence the validation effect (H1), whereas intellectual humility may determine whether increased certainty translates into resistance to subsequent evidence (H2).

These possibilities should be preregistered as distinct interaction hypotheses, with need for cognition and other variables examined exploratorily, because interactions require substantially larger samples than main effects.

The account was developed for ordinary attitudes but bears on clinical reports of what we call, descriptively, delusional spiraling: escalating confidence in an implausible belief over extended chatbot interaction (Morrin et al., 2026; Østergaard, 2023).

Entrenched false beliefs, clinical delusions, and psychotic disorders must not be conflated, and intensive engagement may accompany rather than cause a psychopathological trajectory.

Precision-weighting and aberrant-salience accounts of delusion formation (Adams et al., 2013; Fletcher & Frith, 2009; Kapur, 2003; Sterzer et al., 2018) motivate the comparison without implying equivalence, and schizotypy, loneliness, and insecure attachment are candidate moderators of the validation effect.

text.text: Mandated disagreement is not the answer: it risks performative contrarianism, sycophancy toward the instruction rather than toward the opinion.
The target is calibration: agreement when warranted, well-supported contradiction when the evidence requires it, and expressed uncertainty when evidence is weak.
If a validation effect exists, calibration should be the default rather than an option.
Clinicians will recognize the stance: a delusion is not confronted head-on, but it is not endorsed either.
Convergence is not necessarily improvement.

A system may align users with its own default, which is neither the center of opinion nor necessarily nearer the truth; convergence in decisions (Conlon & Schwardmann, 2026) and depolarization without positional shifts (Kim et al., 2026) cannot alone distinguish learning from homogenization.

text.text: Evaluations should therefore track dispersion across users, accuracy where the model's default is wrong, and confidence separately from position.
Conversational AI can correct or reinforce beliefs, and the evidence so far favors factual content as a major driver.
What remains largely untested is whether approval itself changes how later evidence is received.
We have argued that this question decomposes into two hypotheses, that endorsement raises certainty and that raised certainty slows revision, each of which can be tested, and can fail, on its own.

If the validation effect is negligible, improving evidence quality and its sampling remains the central design target; if it is reproducible, training and interface choices that modulate approval become an additional one.
We therefore recommend measuring position, certainty, and resistance separately in every trial, and testing approval before standardized counterevidence.
Social psychology has long asked where certainty comes from.

Conversational AI makes it possible to separate the informational value of agreement from its social value, and to ask whether non-probative agreement received today makes tomorrow's evidence matter less.
